lessons.summaryHtml: Six days from “I know some Python” to a deployed Django product with a custom dashboard and a REST API a Flutter app can use. Get your machine ready, learn the ground rules, and see the week at a glance.
lessons.contentHtml:
Welcome to the team

You are joining as a Junior Python Developer. Our clients in India, the GCC, the UK and Canada run on systems we build: ERPs, booking apps, LMS platforms, POS systems and SaaS dashboards. This week builds the habits those projects need, not memorised syntax:

  • Correctness first. Money in Decimal, time zones handled, no double bookings.
  • Thin views, fat services. Business rules live in one place and get tested.
  • No Django default admin in production. We build custom, modern dashboards for clients.
  • Ship it. Code isn’t done until it is on Git, tested and deployed.

What you will build: BookIt

From Day 3 every lesson adds a piece to one product: BookIt, a booking platform for a service business (car wash, clinic, salon, gym). We have built this pattern for real clients many times.

Customer (Flutter app) → REST API with JWT → Service layer (rules) → PostgreSQL ← Staff dashboard (Django + Tailwind)

The six days

DayMorning: conceptsAfternoon: real-world taskDeliverable
1 · Python corevenv and Git, mutability, comprehensions, closures, decorators, exceptions, filesDaily Sales Report CLI for a retail POS exportsales_report.py + errors.csv
2 · Professional PythonOOP, dataclasses, typing, Enum, Decimal, generators, context managers, logging, requests, pytestGST Invoice Engine with a full test suiteinvoice.py + passing tests
3 · Django foundationsRequest lifecycle, layout, split settings, PostgreSQL, custom User, models, constraints, migrations, ORMBookIt data layer: models, seed command, 8 report queriesMigrations + seed + reports
4 · Web layer and dashboardURLs, CBVs, templates, forms, auth and roles, service layer, middlewareStaff dashboard with KPIs, search, status workflow, service CRUDWorking dashboard
5 · REST APIsDRF serializers, viewsets, JWT, permissions, throttling, CORS, OpenAPI, API testsMobile API for the Flutter appSwagger docs + green tests
6 · Production and demoProd settings, security checklist, WhiteNoise, Gunicorn, Railway, performance, Git workflowDeploy BookIt, then demo it to the team at 3:00 PMLive URL + demo

A typical day

9:30 – 9:45Stand-up: what I finished, what I’m doing today, what’s blocking me
9:45 – 11:15Concept block 1: the mentor walks through lessons, you type along (no copy-paste)
11:30 – 1:00Concept block 2 + quiz questions in pairs
2:00 – 4:30Real-world task: work independently, commit small and often
4:30 – 5:15Demo and review: 5 minutes each, one mentor comment, one peer comment
5:15 – 5:30Push + daily log: three bullets in LOG.md (learned, built, still unclear)

Ground rules

  • The 20-minute rule. Stuck for 20 minutes? Ask. Bring what you tried, the exact error, and what you expected to happen.
  • Commit every day. Push before 5:30 PM with clear messages (feat: add booking model). Mentors review your PR the next morning.
  • AI tools (Claude Code, Copilot). We use them every day, so you will too. On Days 1–2, write it yourself first, then compare with AI. From Day 3 use AI freely, but you must be able to explain every line in review.
Also post your daily update in the staff portal (Daily updates). It is how your mentor follows your week.

lessons.title: Python traps every junior ships once
lessons.summaryHtml: Mutable default arguments, shallow versus deep copies, and the comprehension and collections tools you will use every day to summarise business data.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Python names point at objects. When two names point at the same list or dict, changing it through one name changes what the other name sees. Most “my cart has items from another customer” bugs come from this one fact.

Trap 1: the mutable default argument

A default value is created once, when the function is defined, not every time it is called. A list default is therefore shared by every call.

def add_item_buggy(item, cart=[]):        # default list is created ONCE
    cart.append(item)
    return cart

def add_item(item, cart=None):            # correct pattern
    if cart is None:
        cart = []
    cart.append(item)
    return cart

print(add_item_buggy("watch"), add_item_buggy("strap"))   # ['watch', 'strap'] twice!
print(add_item("watch"), add_item("strap"))               # ['watch'] ['strap']

Rule: never use a list, dict or set as a default. Use None and create the object inside the function.

Trap 2: shallow copy

copy.copy() copies only the outer container. The inner list of items is still shared. copy.deepcopy() copies all the way down.

order = {"id": 1, "items": [{"sku": "W1", "qty": 1}]}
shallow, deep = copy.copy(order), copy.deepcopy(order)
order["items"][0]["qty"] = 5
print(shallow["items"][0]["qty"], deep["items"][0]["qty"])  # 5 1

Identity, equality and fast lookups

  • == compares values; is compares identity (the same object). Use is only for None, True and False.
  • Immutable: int, float, str, tuple, frozenset, Decimal. Mutable: list, dict, set and most objects.
  • Membership in a set is O(1); in a list it is O(n). Keep “already processed IDs” in a set.
  • sorted(data, key=...) returns a new list; list.sort() sorts in place and returns None.

Summarising data in one line

Business code is mostly “group these rows and add them up”. Learn these tools well:

ToolUse it for
sum(x for x in rows if ...)A total with a filter, without building a list
defaultdict(list)Group rows by a key: order ids per customer
Counter(...)Count by a key; .most_common(n) gives the top n
sorted(rows, key=..., reverse=True)[:n]Top n rows by a field
{k: v for ...} and {x for ...}Dict and set comprehensions: lookup tables and unique values
any() / all()“Is there at least one refunded order?” / “Are all amounts positive?”
paid_total = sum(o["amount"] for o in orders if o["status"] == "paid")
ids_by_customer = defaultdict(list)
for o in orders:
    ids_by_customer[o["customer"]].append(o["id"])
status_count = Counter(o["status"] for o in orders)
top_two = sorted(orders, key=lambda o: o["amount"], reverse=True)[:2]

Unpacking keeps loops readable: first, *rest = ids, and for i, (name, amount) in enumerate(zip(names, amounts), start=1).

Readability check: use a comprehension when it fits on one or two lines and reads like English. If it has two for clauses and an if, write a loop. Your teammate reads code ten times more often than you write it.

The daily workflow

Every Ralfiz project has its own virtual environment and a pinned requirements file. “Works on my machine” is not an acceptable status.

python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
git switch -c feat/sales-report
git add -p && git commit -m "feat: validate sales rows"
Never commit .env files, passwords, API keys, .venv/ or database files. A key leaked in a public repo is abused within minutes.

terms.definition: An object that can change in place: list, dict, set. Strings, ints and tuples are immutable.
A list or dict used as a parameter default. It is created once and shared by every call.
copy.copy(): a new outer object whose inner objects are still shared with the original.
copy.deepcopy(): copies the object and everything inside it.
A comprehension in round brackets, e.g. sum(x for x in rows). It yields values one by one without building a list.
A dict that creates a default value (an empty list, 0) the first time a missing key is used.
A dict subclass that counts things; most_common(n) returns the n most frequent.

lessons.examTip: In interviews, “what does this print?” with a list default argument is one of the most common Python questions. Explain that defaults are evaluated once at definition time.

Explain to yourself why add_item_buggy prints ['watch', 'strap'] twice.
Change the shallow copy example so that changing order no longer affects shallow, without using deepcopy (hint: copy the items list too).
Add a line that prints the total amount per city using defaultdict(int).
Add a line that prints the set of customers who have a paid order, using a set comprehension.

Your per-city totals print Perinthalmanna: 4300, Malappuram: 450, Manjeri: 980.
Your paid-customers set contains only Anu.

quiz.question: def f(x, acc=[]): acc.append(x); return acc. What does print(f(1), f(2)) show?
quiz.explanation: The default list is created once and both calls append to it. Both results are the same list object, printed after both calls ran, so you see [1, 2] twice.

quiz.question: After shallow = copy.copy(order), you change order["items"][0]["qty"]. What happens to shallow?
options: shallow sees the change because the inner list is shared
shallow is reset to an empty dict
quiz.explanation: A shallow copy only copies the outer dict. The items list inside is the same object in both.

quiz.question: Which tool counts orders per status and gives the most common one?
quiz.explanation: Counter(o["status"] for o in orders).most_common(1) counts and ranks in one step.

quiz.question: What is the safest default for a parameter that should start as an empty list?
options: cart=None, then create the list inside
quiz.explanation: Use None as the default and create a fresh list inside the function on each call.

quiz.question: When should you use is instead of ==?
options: Only for singletons such as None, True and False
quiz.explanation: == checks equal values; is checks the same object in memory. Two equal strings or numbers may be different objects.

lessons.title: Functions, decorators and exceptions
lessons.summaryHtml: Keyword-only arguments, closures, the @timed and @retry decorators you will meet in real code, and an exception hierarchy that callers can catch cleanly.
lessons.contentHtml:
Keyword-only arguments

Everything after a bare * must be passed by name. This stops callers from mixing up two string arguments.

def send_sms(phone, message, *, sender="RALFIZ", **meta):
    """sender is keyword-only: send_sms("98..", "hi", "X") is an error -> fewer bugs."""
    return f"[{sender}] to {phone}: {message} {meta or ''}".strip()

send_sms("9895663498", "Your booking is confirmed", sender="BOOKIT", booking_id=42)

**meta collects any extra keyword arguments into a dict, here {'booking_id': 42}.

Closures

An inner function remembers the variables of the function that created it. That lets you build configured functions.

def make_discount(percent):
    def apply(amount):
        return round(amount * (100 - percent) / 100, 2)
    return apply

festival = make_discount(10)
festival(1999)   # 1799.1

Decorators

A decorator is a function that takes a function and returns a new one that wraps it. Django uses them everywhere: @login_required, @require_POST, @transaction.atomic. Writing two yourself makes them stop feeling like magic.

def timed(func):
    @functools.wraps(func)               # keeps func.__name__ / docstring
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        start = time.perf_counter()
        try:
            return func(*args, **kwargs)
        finally:
            logger.info("%s took %.1f ms", func.__name__, (time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000)
    return wrapper

@retry(times=3, exceptions=(ConnectionError,)) takes arguments, so it is a function that returns a decorator: three levels deep. It retries only the exceptions you name, waits a little longer each time (backoff), and re-raises on the last attempt so failures are never swallowed.

Always use functools.wraps. Without it every decorated function is called wrapper in logs and tracebacks.

Exceptions with meaning

Create one base class per area and specific subclasses under it. Callers catch the base class; the message is safe to show.

class PaymentError(Exception):
    """Base class for all payment problems."""

class InsufficientBalance(PaymentError):
    def __init__(self, needed, available):
        super().__init__(f"Need Rs {needed}, wallet has Rs {available}")
        self.needed, self.available = needed, available

try:
    pay_from_wallet(500, 120)
except PaymentError as exc:              # catch the family, not bare `except:`
    print("Payment failed:", exc)
else:
    print("runs only when no exception")
finally:
    print("always runs: close files, release locks")

Never write a bare except:. It also catches KeyboardInterrupt and hides real bugs.

terms.definition: A parameter after * in the signature; it can only be passed as name=value.
Collects extra keyword arguments into a dict.
An inner function that keeps access to variables of the function that created it.
A function that wraps another function to add behaviour before or after it, applied with @name.
Copies the wrapped function’s name and docstring onto the wrapper.
Waiting longer between each retry so a struggling server gets time to recover.
A base exception class with specific subclasses, so callers can catch a whole family.

lessons.examTip: Stacked decorators apply bottom-up: in @timed over @retry, retry wraps the function first and timed measures all the attempts together.

steps: Run python fundamentals.py and find the two WARNING lines from @retry and the INFO line from @timed.
Swap the order of @timed and @retry. Run again and explain why the timing line now appears differently.
Call send_sms("9895663498", "hi", "X") and read the TypeError. Fix the call by passing sender by name.
Write a decorator log_calls that logs the function name and its arguments before calling it. Apply it to pay_from_wallet.
Add a CardDeclined(PaymentError) exception and raise it from a new pay_by_card function. Catch it with the existing except PaymentError block.
check: The script ends with SUCCESS after 3 attempts and Payment failed: Need Rs 500, wallet has Rs 120.
With the decorators swapped you see one timing line per attempt instead of one in total.
Your CardDeclined is caught by except PaymentError without adding a new except branch.

quiz.question: def send_sms(phone, message, *, sender="RALFIZ"). Which call is valid?
quiz.explanation: sender comes after *, so it must be passed by name. phone and message are required.

quiz.question: Why use functools.wraps inside a decorator?
options: It keeps the original function name and docstring
It is required for the decorator to run
quiz.explanation: Without wraps the decorated function reports its name as wrapper, which makes logs and debugging confusing.

quiz.question: A retry decorator should re-raise the exception on the last attempt because…
options: otherwise a real failure would be silently swallowed
quiz.explanation: If the final attempt fails the caller must know. Returning None would hide the outage.

quiz.question: Which block runs whether or not an exception was raised?
quiz.explanation: finally always runs. else runs only when no exception occurred.

lessons.title: Project: daily sales report from a CSV
lessons.summaryHtml: A real command-line tool: read a POS export, validate every row, reject bad rows with a reason, and write a JSON summary. Dataclasses, Decimal, argparse and pathlib.
lessons.contentHtml:
The job

A shop sends you its daily POS export. Some rows are broken: a missing quantity, abc as a price, a negative quantity. The tool must never crash on bad data. It keeps the good rows, explains every bad one, and produces totals.

python sales_report.py data/sales.csv --out report.json --top 5

Model the row with a frozen dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Sale:
    invoice_no: str
    date: str
    product: str
    qty: int
    unit_price: Decimal
    payment_mode: str

    @property
    def total(self) -> Decimal:
        return self.unit_price * self.qty

frozen=True means a Sale cannot be changed after it is created. A computed value such as total is a @property, so it can never get out of step with qty and price.

Money is Decimal, never float

0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004 in float. On an invoice that is a wrong rupee figure. Parse prices with Decimal("2450.00") (from the string, not from a float).

Validate in one place and raise a meaningful error

def parse_row(row: dict[str, str]) -> Sale:
    missing = [key for key in REQUIRED if not (row.get(key) or "").strip()]
    if missing:
        raise RowError(f"missing {', '.join(missing)}")
    try:
        qty = int(row["qty"])
        price = Decimal(row["unit_price"])
    except (ValueError, InvalidOperation) as exc:
        raise RowError("bad number in qty/unit_price") from exc
    if qty <= 0 or price < 0:
        raise RowError("qty must be > 0 and unit_price >= 0")
    ...

raise ... from exc keeps the original error attached for debugging. The loader catches only RowError, records the line number (enumerate(..., start=2) because line 1 is the header) and moves on.

Clean the data while parsing

The export has UPI, upi and Cash. .strip().upper() normalises the payment mode so the summary groups them correctly.

A testable main()

main(argv=None) parses arguments and returns an exit code, and the file ends with sys.exit(main()). A test can call main(["data/sales.csv", "--top", "3"]) directly without starting a new process.

Money totals are written to JSON as strings (str(Decimal)). JSON has no decimal type, and a float would bring the rounding problem back.

The brief

A watch retailer exports sales from their POS as CSV every evening. The owner wants a summary on WhatsApp each night, and the accountant wants every bad row explained.

Acceptance criteria (mentor checks at 4:30)

  • Grand total for the sample is exactly 14347.00, with 3 rejected rows (lines 6, 7, 9).
  • No float anywhere in money calculations.
  • A custom RowError exception; no bare except.
  • Small functions, one job each: parse, load, summarise, write.
  • Committed on branch feat/sales-report and pushed.

Stretch goals: a --date filter; a WhatsApp-ready text summary with ₹ formatting; three pytest tests for parse_row.

terms.definition: A class decorator that writes __init__, __repr__ and __eq__ for you from typed fields.
A dataclass whose fields cannot be reassigned after creation.
Exact base-10 numbers from the decimal module. Use for money; never float.
Reads a CSV file and gives each row as a dict keyed by the header names.
The standard library module for command-line arguments and --help.
0 means success; any other number tells the shell or a scheduler that the run failed.
raise NewError(...) from exc keeps the original exception as the cause.

lessons.examTip: If an interviewer asks how you handle money in Python, answer: Decimal created from strings, quantize to two places with ROUND_HALF_UP, and store as a decimal column in the database.

Open out/report.json and out/errors.csv. Match each rejected line in errors.csv with the broken row in sales.csv.
Add a new rule: a payment_mode that is not UPI, CASH or CARD is rejected with the message "unknown payment mode".
Add a row INV-1009,2026-11-03,Wall Clock,1,899.00,Cheque to sales.csv and confirm it lands in errors.csv.
Add a "by_date" section to the summary with the revenue for each date.
Run python sales_report.py missing.csv and check that it logs an error and returns exit code 1 (echo $? on Mac/Linux).
check: Before your changes: Valid rows: 6 | Rejected: 3 and Grand total: Rs 14347.00.
by_payment_mode shows CARD 2800.00, CASH 2649.00 and UPI 8898.00 (upi and UPI are grouped).
After adding the Cheque row, Rejected becomes 4 and the grand total does not change.

quiz.question: Why is unit_price parsed with Decimal(row["unit_price"]) instead of float()?
options: float cannot represent values like 0.1 exactly, so money totals drift
quiz.explanation: Binary floating point cannot store most decimal fractions exactly. Decimal does base-10 arithmetic like an accountant.

quiz.question: Why does enumerate(csv.DictReader(f), start=2) start at 2?
options: Line 1 of the file is the header, so the first data row is line 2
To skip the first data row
quiz.explanation: Reporting the real file line number lets the shop find and fix the row.

quiz.question: What does frozen=True on the Sale dataclass give you?
options: Sales cannot be modified after creation
quiz.explanation: A frozen dataclass raises an error if you try to reassign a field, so a parsed sale stays exactly as validated.

quiz.question: Why does main() accept argv and return an int?
options: So tests can call it directly and check the exit code
quiz.explanation: A main that takes argv and returns an exit code is easy to test and works with sys.exit for the shell.

lessons.title: Project: a GST invoice engine
lessons.summaryHtml: Pure-Python invoicing as Indian businesses need it: CGST + SGST inside the state, IGST across states, round-off to the rupee, GSTIN validation and financial-year invoice numbers.
lessons.contentHtml:
Classes that model the business

  • Class = a noun in the domain (Invoice, LineItem, Party). Method = a verb it can do (add, totals).
  • @property exposes calculated values (taxable_value) that read like attributes and are always up to date.
  • @classmethod for alternative constructors (Invoice.from_dict(...)); @staticmethod for helpers that need neither the instance nor the class.
  • Dunder methods make objects feel native: __str__ for users, __repr__ for developers, __eq__ for comparisons.
  • Prefer composition over inheritance. An Invoice has LineItems; it is not a kind of list.
  • In a dataclass, a list field needs field(default_factory=list). It is the dataclass version of the mutable default bug from Day 1.
  • Type hints (list[LineItem], str | None) are documentation the editor checks for you.

The rules

  • Money is always Decimal, rounded ROUND_HALF_UP to 2 places.
  • Seller and buyer in the same state (same state code): CGST + SGST, half the rate each.
  • Different states: IGST at the full rate.
  • The grand total is rounded to the nearest rupee; the difference is shown as round_off.
  • Invoice numbers follow the Indian financial year (April to March): RLZ/2026-27/0001.

Rounding in one helper

PAISA = Decimal("0.01")

def money(value: Decimal) -> Decimal:
    return value.quantize(PAISA, rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP)

Python’s default rounding is banker’s rounding (round(2.5) == 2). Accountants expect half-up. Putting it in one function means nobody rounds differently by accident.

Validate when the object is created

__post_init__ runs right after a dataclass’s generated __init__. An invalid party or line item can never exist.

GSTIN_RE = re.compile(r"^\d{2}[A-Z]{5}\d{4}[A-Z][1-9A-Z]Z[0-9A-Z]$")

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Party:
    name: str
    state_code: str  # "32" = Kerala, "29" = Karnataka ...
    gstin: str | None = None

    def __post_init__(self) -> None:
        if self.gstin:
            if not GSTIN_RE.match(self.gstin):
                raise ValueError(f"Invalid GSTIN: {self.gstin}")
            if self.gstin[:2] != self.state_code:
                raise ValueError("GSTIN state code does not match party state")

The first two digits of a GSTIN are the state code, so a Karnataka party with a 32… GSTIN is rejected.

An Enum instead of magic strings

class SupplyType(str, Enum):
    INTRA = "intra"  # CGST + SGST
    INTER = "inter"  # IGST

Invoice.supply_type is a property derived from the two state codes. It is never stored, so it can never be wrong.

The financial year

def financial_year(d: date) -> str:
    """Indian FY runs April -> March. 9 Nov 2026 -> '2026-27'."""
    start = d.year if d.month >= 4 else d.year - 1
    return f"{start}-{str(start + 1)[-2:]}"
The InvoiceNumberGenerator here keeps its counter in memory. In Django two users saving at the same moment could get the same number. The fix is a database row locked with select_for_update(), which you will see in lesson 4.1.
GST slabs change by government notification. In real projects keep the allowed rates in settings or the database and confirm them with the accountant.

terms.definition: Central and State GST, each half of the rate, charged when seller and buyer are in the same state.
Integrated GST at the full rate, charged on supplies between different states.
The 15-character GST number. Its first two digits are the state code (32 = Kerala).
Codes that classify goods (HSN) and services (SAC) on a GST invoice.
Rounding where .5 always goes up, the way accountants round.
A dataclass hook that runs after __init__; the place for validation.
India’s accounting year, 1 April to 31 March, written as 2026-27.

lessons.examTip: Taxable value is computed per line before tax; tax is then calculated on each line and added up. Rounding each step to paise in one helper keeps the invoice matching the accountant’s figures.

quiz.explanation: Different state codes mean an inter-state supply, so IGST at the full rate.

quiz.question: What does financial_year(date(2026, 3, 31)) return?
quiz.explanation: March is before April, so the year started in April 2025: 2025-26.

quiz.question: Why is validation in __post_init__ instead of a separate validate() method?
options: An invalid object can never be created, so nobody can forget to call validate()
dataclasses do not allow other methods
quiz.explanation: Validating at construction makes invalid states impossible rather than merely discouraged.

quiz.question: Why does Invoice use items: list[LineItem] = field(default_factory=list)?
options: A plain = [] would be shared by every invoice; the factory makes a fresh list each time
quiz.explanation: Dataclasses refuse a bare mutable default for exactly this reason. default_factory creates a new list per instance.

quiz.question: Why does the engine return Decimal values and not formatted strings like "₹11,800.00"?
options: Keep data and presentation separate: templates, PDFs and APIs decide the formatting
quiz.explanation: The engine computes exact values. Each place that shows them formats them for its own audience.

quiz.question: Why is the in-memory InvoiceNumberGenerator not safe in a web app?
options: Several server processes and simultaneous requests could hand out the same number
quiz.explanation: Each worker process has its own counter, and two requests can race. A locked database row gives one shared, ordered sequence.

lessons.title: Testing with pytest
lessons.summaryHtml: Prove the invoice engine is right and keep it right: plain assert, fixtures, @pytest.mark.parametrize for edge cases, and pytest.raises for rules that must fail.
lessons.contentHtml:
Why tests

Tax rules have edge cases: the last day of March, paise that round up, an interstate client. You will change this code later. Tests are how you know you did not break last month’s invoices.

A test is a function that asserts

def test_intra_state_splits_cgst_and_sgst(web_item):
    t = make_invoice("32").add(web_item).totals()
    assert t["cgst"] == t["sgst"] == Decimal("900.00")
    assert t["igst"] == Decimal("0.00")
    assert t["grand_total"] == Decimal("11800.00")

Name tests after the rule they prove. When one fails, the name tells you which business rule broke.

Fixtures: shared setup

@pytest.fixture
def web_item() -> LineItem:
    return LineItem("Website development", "998314", 1, Decimal("10000"), Decimal("18"))

A test that has a parameter named web_item receives a fresh one. Each test gets its own object, so tests never affect each other.

parametrize: one test, many cases

@pytest.mark.parametrize(
    "day, expected",
    [(date(2026, 3, 31), "2025-26"), (date(2026, 4, 1), "2026-27"), (date(2027, 1, 15), "2026-27")],
)
def test_financial_year(day, expected):
    assert financial_year(day) == expected

Always test the boundary: 31 March and 1 April are where an off-by-one bug would hide.

Testing that bad input is rejected

@pytest.mark.parametrize("kwargs", [{"qty": 0}, {"gst_rate": Decimal("7")}, {"discount": Decimal("-1")}])
def test_invalid_line_items_rejected(kwargs):
    data = {"description": "x", "hsn_sac": "1", "qty": 1, "unit_price": Decimal("100"), "gst_rate": Decimal("18")}
    data.update(kwargs)
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        LineItem(**data)

Running

pip install pytest
pytest -q                 # all tests, quiet
pytest -k financial -v    # only tests whose name contains "financial"
pytest -x                 # stop at the first failure
Write the test for a bug before you fix the bug. If the test fails first and passes after the fix, you know you fixed the right thing.

terms.definition: Python’s most used test runner. It finds test_*.py files and functions named test_*.
A function decorated with @pytest.fixture that builds test data; tests receive it by naming it as a parameter.
Runs one test function once per set of inputs.
A context manager that passes only if the code inside raises the given exception.
An input at the boundary of a rule, such as 31 March or a zero quantity.
A test written for a bug that was fixed, so it can never come back unnoticed.

lessons.examTip: Good tests check behaviour (the totals a customer sees), not implementation details (which private helper was called). That is what lets you refactor safely.

steps: In the day2 folder run pip install pytest and then pytest -q. All tests should pass.
Break the code on purpose: change ROUND_HALF_UP to ROUND_DOWN in money(). Run pytest and read which test fails and why. Undo the change.
Add a test that an interstate invoice with two items sums the IGST of both lines.
Add a parametrized test for Party GSTIN validation with one valid and two invalid GSTINs.
Write a test for the amount_in_words() method you added in lesson 2.1.
check: pytest -q reports 11 passed for the original file.
With ROUND_DOWN, test_round_off_to_nearest_rupee fails.
Your new tests pass, and pytest -q now reports more than 11 passed.

quiz.question: How does a test function receive a fixture?
options: By having a parameter with the fixture’s name
quiz.explanation: pytest looks at the test’s parameter names and injects the matching fixtures.

quiz.question: Which dates best test financial_year()?
quiz.explanation: Bugs hide at boundaries. The FY changes between 31 March and 1 April.

quiz.question: with pytest.raises(ValueError): LineItem(qty=0, ...) passes when…
quiz.explanation: pytest.raises passes only if that exception type is raised inside the block.

quiz.question: What does @pytest.mark.parametrize do?
options: Runs the same test once for each input set
quiz.explanation: Each tuple of values becomes a separate test case with its own pass or fail.

lessons.title: Calling real APIs safely
lessons.summaryHtml: Address autofill from a PIN code: a reusable requests.Session, automatic retries with backoff, timeouts on every call, a timing context manager, and a generator for files too big for memory.
lessons.contentHtml:
The feature

On a booking or checkout form the customer types a 6-digit PIN code and the district and state fill in. Your code calls a public API, and public APIs are slow, flaky and sometimes down.

Validate before you call

if not (pin.isdigit() and len(pin) == 6):
    raise ValueError("PIN code must be 6 digits")

Never send a request you already know is wrong. It wastes time and counts against rate limits.

A session with retries

def build_session() -> requests.Session:
    session = requests.Session()
    retry = Retry(total=3, backoff_factor=0.5, status_forcelist=(429, 500, 502, 503, 504), allowed_methods=("GET",))
    session.mount("https://", HTTPAdapter(max_retries=retry))
    session.headers.update({"Accept": "application/json", "User-Agent": "bookit/1.0"})
    return session

A session reuses the TCP connection between calls. The retry policy handles “server busy” (429) and server errors (5xx) automatically, waiting longer each time. It only retries GET, because retrying a POST could charge a customer twice.

ALWAYS set a timeout

resp = session.get(API.format(pin=pin), timeout=(3, 10))  # (connect, read) seconds
Without a timeout, requests can wait forever. One hung API call holds a web worker, and a few of them take your whole site down.

Check the answer, not just the status code

resp.raise_for_status()
payload = resp.json()[0]
if payload.get("Status") != "Success" or not payload.get("PostOffice"):
    raise PincodeNotFound(pin)
return [PostOffice(p["Name"], p["District"], p["State"]) for p in payload["PostOffice"]]

This API returns HTTP 200 even for an unknown PIN, with "Status": "Error" in the body. Convert the raw JSON into your own small dataclass so the rest of the code does not depend on the API’s field names.

logging, not print

Use logger = logging.getLogger(__name__) and lazy formatting: logger.info("pin=%s", pin), not an f-string. Logs carry a level and a source, can be switched off per module, and go to Railway’s log viewer in production. print does none of that.

Context managers and generators

@contextmanager turns a function with one yield into a with block. The timer logs how long the block took, even if it raised.

A generator function uses yield to hand back one batch at a time. read_in_batches() can process a 2 GB log file using the memory of 1,000 lines.

def read_in_batches(path: str, size: int = 1000):
    batch = []
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for line in f:
            batch.append(line.rstrip("\n"))
            if len(batch) == size:
                yield batch
                batch = []
    if batch:
        yield batch

terms.definition: Reuses connections and shared headers across many HTTP calls.
The longest time to wait to connect and to read. Always pass one to requests.
urllib3’s Retry repeats failed requests, waiting longer each time.
Safe to repeat: GET is, a payment POST is not. Only retry idempotent requests automatically.
Raises an HTTPError for 4xx and 5xx responses.
An object used with with that runs setup and guaranteed cleanup code.
A function that yields values lazily, one at a time, instead of returning a full list.

lessons.examTip: “What happens if the third-party API is down?” is a standard design question. Answer with timeouts, limited retries with backoff for idempotent calls, a clear error to the user, and logging.

steps: pip install requests, then run python pincode_client.py. It looks up PIN 679322 and logs how long it took.
Call lookup("12345") and lookup("000000") in a Python shell. Note which raises ValueError and which raises PincodeNotFound.
Add a simple cache: a dict in the module that returns the stored answer for a PIN already looked up. Log "cache hit" when it is used.
Change the timeout to (0.001, 0.001) and run again. Read the exception, then put the timeout back.
Write a function count_lines(path) that uses read_in_batches() to count lines in a large file without loading it.
check: lookup("679322") returns post offices in Malappuram district, Kerala.
A second lookup of the same PIN logs "cache hit" and takes under 1 ms.
The tiny timeout raises a requests ConnectTimeout or ReadTimeout instead of hanging.

quiz.question: What can happen if you call requests.get() without a timeout?
options: The call can wait forever and block a web worker
Nothing, requests always has a timeout
quiz.explanation: requests has no default timeout. A hung call ties up the worker until the server or the process gives up.

quiz.question: Why does the Retry policy only allow GET?
options: GET is idempotent; retrying a POST could create a second order or payment
quiz.explanation: Only safe, repeatable requests should be retried automatically.

quiz.question: The PIN API returns HTTP 200 for an unknown PIN. How does the client detect it?
options: By checking payload["Status"] and that PostOffice is not empty
quiz.explanation: Some APIs report errors in the body, so the client checks the body as well as the status code.

quiz.question: Why use a generator to read a 2 GB file?
options: It is the only way to open files
It keeps only one batch in memory at a time
quiz.explanation: A generator yields one batch at a time, so memory use stays small whatever the file size.

domains.blurb: BookIt set up for production, models that protect the data, and the queries behind every report.

lessons.title: A Django project laid out for production
lessons.summaryHtml: BookIt, a booking system for a car-wash business, set up the way Ralfiz projects are: split settings, secrets from .env, apps under apps/, a custom User model from day one, and a small middleware.
lessons.contentHtml:
The project

For the rest of the course you work on BookIt: customers book services (Full Car Wash, Interior Detailing), staff manage bookings in a dashboard, and a mobile app talks to a REST API. Download the whole project from the course page (Course files).

bookit/
  config/
    settings/base.py  dev.py  prod.py
    urls.py  wsgi.py
  apps/
    core/        TimeStampedModel, middleware
    accounts/    custom User with roles
    catalog/     Service
    bookings/    Booking, services.py (business rules)
    dashboard/   staff web pages
    api/         DRF API for the app
  templates/
  requirements/base.txt  dev.txt  prod.txt
  .env.example  manage.py  pytest.ini

How a request flows through Django

Browser / Flutter app → Gunicorn → Middleware → URLconf → View → Service layer → Model / ORM → PostgreSQL, and the response travels back through the middleware in reverse order. When something breaks, ask which layer it broke in. That one question solves half of all debugging.

Project = configuration (config/). App = one business area (bookings, catalog). MVT: Model (data), View (request → response logic), Template (HTML).

Split settings

base.py holds everything shared. dev.py and prod.py start with from .base import * and change only what differs: DEBUG, allowed hosts, HTTPS, static storage.

Secrets come from the environment

env = environ.Env(DEBUG=(bool, False))
environ.Env.read_env(BASE_DIR / ".env")

SECRET_KEY = env("SECRET_KEY")
DEBUG = env("DEBUG")
DATABASES = {"default": env.db("DATABASE_URL")}

The real .env is never committed; .env.example shows which variables exist. DEBUG defaults to False, so forgetting it in production is safe.

  • USE_TZ = True and TIME_ZONE = "Asia/Kolkata": the database stores UTC and users see IST. Gulf and UK clients just change the display zone.
  • django.contrib.admin is not installed. Clients get a custom dashboard (Day 4).

A custom User from day one

class User(AbstractUser):
    """Custom user from day one — changing AUTH_USER_MODEL later is painful."""

    class Role(models.TextChoices):
        ADMIN = "admin", "Admin"
        STAFF = "staff", "Staff"
        CUSTOMER = "customer", "Customer"

    role = models.CharField(max_length=20, choices=Role.choices, default=Role.CUSTOMER)
    phone = models.CharField(max_length=15, unique=True, null=True, blank=True)

    @property
    def is_staff_member(self) -> bool:
        return self.role in {self.Role.ADMIN, self.Role.STAFF}

Set AUTH_USER_MODEL = "accounts.User" before the first migration. Switching later means rewriting every foreign key to users. Note phone is null=True with unique=True: many users may have no phone, and NULLs do not clash, but empty strings would.

Middleware

Middleware wraps every request. SlowRequestLogMiddleware times the request, logs any slower than 500 ms and adds an X-Response-Time-ms header.

class SlowRequestLogMiddleware:
    def __init__(self, get_response):
        self.get_response = get_response

    def __call__(self, request):
        start = time.perf_counter()
        response = self.get_response(request)
        elapsed_ms = (time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000
        if elapsed_ms > SLOW_MS:
            logger.warning("SLOW %s %s took %.0f ms", request.method, request.path, elapsed_ms)
        response["X-Response-Time-ms"] = f"{elapsed_ms:.0f}"
        return response

Run it

python -m venv venv && source venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements/dev.txt
cp .env.example .env            # then edit DATABASE_URL and SECRET_KEY
export DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=config.settings.dev
python manage.py migrate
python manage.py seed_demo
python manage.py createsuperuser   # then set role="admin" in the shell
python manage.py runserver
No PostgreSQL on your laptop yet? Set DATABASE_URL=sqlite:///db.sqlite3 in .env to start. The course uses PostgreSQL in production, like Ralfiz BMS on Railway.

terms.definition: A settings package with base.py plus one file per environment that imports from base.
Reads settings such as SECRET_KEY and DATABASE_URL from environment variables or a .env file.
The setting that points Django at your custom User model. Set it before the first migrate.
A Django enum for a field’s allowed values and their human labels.
A class that runs code before and after every request and response.
A Django package for one area of the business (catalog, bookings) with its own models and migrations.

lessons.examTip: If asked “why a custom user model?”, say: Django’s own docs recommend it for every new project, because adding fields like role or phone later requires a painful migration.

steps: Download the full BookIt project from Course files on the course page and unzip it.
Create a virtual environment, install requirements/dev.txt, copy .env.example to .env and set DATABASE_URL (SQLite is fine to start).
Run migrate, then seed_demo, then runserver with DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=config.settings.dev.
Create a superuser, then in python manage.py shell set its role to "admin" and save it. Log in at /accounts/login/.
Open any page and find the X-Response-Time-ms header in the browser’s Network tab.
Add a LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG line to .env and restart. Notice how much more is logged, then set it back to INFO.
check: seed_demo prints Seeded 200 bookings, 10 customers.
You can log in and see the Overview page with four numbers.
Every response has an X-Response-Time-ms header.

quiz.question: Why must AUTH_USER_MODEL be set before the first migration?
options: Every foreign key to users is created against it; changing it later means rewriting those tables
It is required for the admin
quiz.explanation: Migrations bake the user table into every relation. Changing the model after data exists is a hard, risky migration.

quiz.question: Where should SECRET_KEY come from in production?
quiz.explanation: Secrets live in the environment (Railway variables, a local .env) and are never committed to git.

quiz.question: Why is phone defined with null=True as well as unique=True?
options: Many users have no phone; NULLs do not clash under a unique constraint but empty strings would
quiz.explanation: Two empty strings are equal and would break uniqueness. Two NULLs are not considered equal.

quiz.question: What does middleware wrap?
options: Every request and response passing through Django
quiz.explanation: Each middleware runs around every request, which is why it suits timing, security headers and confinement rules.

lessons.title: Models that protect your data
lessons.summaryHtml: Service and Booking: a timestamp base class, TextChoices, a price snapshot, on_delete choices, indexes, a database CheckConstraint and a tiny status state machine.
lessons.contentHtml:
A base class for every table

class TimeStampedModel(models.Model):
    created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)
    updated_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now=True)

    class Meta:
        abstract = True

abstract = True means no table of its own; every model that inherits gets the two columns.

The Booking model

class Booking(TimeStampedModel):
    class Status(models.TextChoices):
        PENDING = "pending", "Pending"
        CONFIRMED = "confirmed", "Confirmed"
        COMPLETED = "completed", "Completed"
        CANCELLED = "cancelled", "Cancelled"

    customer = models.ForeignKey(settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL, on_delete=models.PROTECT, related_name="bookings")
    staff = models.ForeignKey(settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL, on_delete=models.SET_NULL, null=True, blank=True,
                              related_name="assigned_bookings", limit_choices_to={"role": "staff"})
    service = models.ForeignKey(Service, on_delete=models.PROTECT, related_name="bookings")
    start_at = models.DateTimeField()
    end_at = models.DateTimeField()
    status = models.CharField(max_length=20, choices=Status.choices, default=Status.PENDING)
    # Snapshot of the price at booking time — later price changes must not rewrite history
    price = models.DecimalField(max_digits=10, decimal_places=2)

on_delete is a business decision

ChoiceMeaning here
PROTECTYou cannot delete a customer or service that has bookings. Revenue history must survive.
SET_NULLIf a staff member leaves, their bookings stay with no staff assigned.
CASCADEDelete the children too. Fine for things like a booking’s notes, dangerous for money.

Snapshot the price

The service price will go up next year. Last year’s bookings must still show what the customer actually paid, so the booking copies the price when it is created instead of reading service.price later.

Rules the database enforces

class Meta:
    ordering = ["-start_at"]
    indexes = [
        models.Index(fields=["status", "start_at"]),
        models.Index(fields=["service", "start_at"]),
    ]
    constraints = [
        models.CheckConstraint(condition=Q(end_at__gt=F("start_at")), name="booking_end_after_start"),
    ]

Python validation can be skipped by a bulk update, a shell session or another program. A CheckConstraint cannot. The indexes match the dashboard’s most common filters: by status and date, and by service and date.

A status state machine

ALLOWED_TRANSITIONS = {
    Status.PENDING: {Status.CONFIRMED, Status.CANCELLED},
    Status.CONFIRMED: {Status.COMPLETED, Status.CANCELLED},
    Status.COMPLETED: set(),
    Status.CANCELLED: set(),
}

def can_transition_to(self, new_status: str) -> bool:
    return new_status in self.ALLOWED_TRANSITIONS[self.status]

A completed booking can never be cancelled and a cancelled one can never be completed. The rule lives in one dictionary that anyone can read.

The Service model has its own constraint: CheckConstraint(condition=Q(price__gte=0), name="service_price_non_negative"). Every rule that must never break belongs in the database.

Migrations: the rules

  • Commit migration files with the model change, in the same PR.
  • Never edit a migration that has already run on a shared database or in production. Create a new one.
  • Two people changing the same app at once causes migration conflicts. Talk before touching models.
  • Adding a non-null column to a big table needs a default or a 3-step migration. Ask a senior first.

The brief: BookIt data layer

A car wash chain wants online bookings. Today you deliver the database design and the reports the owner asked for in the kickoff meeting. Acceptance: python manage.py check is clean and migrations are committed; saving a booking with end_at before start_at raises IntegrityError; deleting a booked service raises ProtectedError.

Stretch goal: use PostgreSQL’s ExclusionConstraint (from django.contrib.postgres) to make overlapping active bookings for the same service impossible at the database level.

terms.definition: A base model with Meta.abstract = True; it adds fields to subclasses but has no table.
What happens to rows pointing at a deleted row: PROTECT, CASCADE, SET_NULL and others.
The name for the reverse relation, e.g. service.bookings.all().
A rule enforced by the database itself on every insert and update.
A database structure that makes filtering and sorting on given columns fast.
Copying a value at the time of a transaction so later changes do not rewrite history.
A fixed set of states and the allowed moves between them.

lessons.examTip: When asked about on_delete, give a reason per relation. Choosing CASCADE on a customer that has invoices is a classic way to lose financial data.

steps: Open apps/bookings/models.py and apps/catalog/models.py and match each field to a column in migrations/0001_initial.py.
In python manage.py shell, try to delete a service that has bookings. Read the ProtectedError.
Try Booking.objects.filter(pk=1).update(end_at=F("start_at")). Read the IntegrityError from the constraint.
Add a NO_SHOW status that is allowed only from CONFIRMED. Update ALLOWED_TRANSITIONS and run makemigrations.
Add a discount DecimalField to Booking with a CheckConstraint that it is between 0 and price. Run makemigrations and migrate.
check: Deleting a booked service raises ProtectedError and the service still exists.
The update that sets end_at equal to start_at fails with an IntegrityError naming booking_end_after_start.
Your new migration applies cleanly and Booking.Status.NO_SHOW exists.

quiz.question: Why does Booking store its own price instead of reading service.price?
options: So a later price change does not rewrite what past customers paid
Because DecimalField cannot be a foreign key
quiz.explanation: The booking keeps a snapshot of the agreed price. Reports and invoices for old bookings stay correct.

quiz.question: Which on_delete stops you deleting a customer who has bookings?
quiz.explanation: PROTECT raises ProtectedError while related rows exist.

quiz.question: Why use a CheckConstraint when the form already validates end_at > start_at?
options: The database enforces it for every write, including bulk updates and scripts that skip the form
quiz.explanation: Code paths that bypass forms still cannot write invalid rows.

quiz.question: With the ALLOWED_TRANSITIONS shown, which move is allowed?
quiz.explanation: Pending can become confirmed or cancelled. Completed and cancelled are final.

quiz.question: A migration has already run on production and has a mistake. What do you do?
options: Edit the migration file and redeploy
Write a new migration that fixes it
quiz.explanation: Production has recorded that migration as applied, so edits never run there. Fix forward with a new migration.

lessons.title: ORM reports and the N+1 problem
lessons.summaryHtml: The queries behind every dashboard: select_related, aggregate, annotate with conditional counts, group-by-date, Q searches, F updates, and measuring the N+1 problem yourself.
lessons.contentHtml:
Think in queries, not loops

The database is far better at filtering, counting and adding up than a Python loop. Every report below is a single SQL query. Paste them into python manage.py shell one by one and print .query to see the SQL.

Aggregate: one number

month = Booking.objects.filter(
    status=S.COMPLETED, start_at__year=today.year, start_at__month=today.month
).aggregate(revenue=Sum("price"), jobs=Count("id"))
# a dict: {'revenue': Decimal(...), 'jobs': ...}

Annotate: a number per row

popular = Service.objects.annotate(
    total=Count("bookings"),
    cancelled=Count("bookings", filter=Q(bookings__status=S.CANCELLED)),
).order_by("-total")

The filter=Q(...) inside Count gives a conditional count in the same query.

Group by date for a chart

daily = (
    Booking.objects.filter(status=S.COMPLETED, start_at__date__gte=today - timedelta(days=30))
    .annotate(day=TruncDate("start_at"))
    .values("day")
    .annotate(revenue=Sum("price"))
    .order_by("day")
)

The pattern .values(<group>).annotate(<aggregate>) is SQL’s GROUP BY.

Search across relations

found = Booking.objects.filter(
    Q(customer__first_name__icontains=q) | Q(customer__phone__icontains=q) | Q(service__name__icontains=q)
)

Update in the database with F()

Service.objects.filter(slug="bike-wash").update(price=F("price") + Decimal("20"))

Reading the price into Python, adding 20 and saving would lose a change made by someone else at the same moment. F() does the arithmetic inside the database in one statement.

The N+1 problem, measured

reset_queries()
for b in Booking.objects.all()[:50]:
    _ = (b.customer.first_name, b.service.name)   # each access = a new query
print("without select_related:", len(connection.queries))  # 101

reset_queries()
for b in Booking.objects.select_related("customer", "service")[:50]:
    _ = (b.customer.first_name, b.service.name)
print("with select_related:", len(connection.queries))     # 1

One query for the bookings plus one per booking for the customer and one for the service: 1 + 50 + 50 = 101. select_related joins them into a single query. Use it for foreign keys you will display; use prefetch_related for reverse and many-to-many relations.

A page that is fast with 10 rows in development and slow with 5,000 in production is almost always N+1. Check with django-debug-toolbar (in requirements/dev.txt).

terms.definition: A lazy description of a query; it runs only when you iterate, slice with a step, count or print it.
Returns a dict of totals over the whole QuerySet.
Adds a computed value to every row (or every group after values()).
A filter condition that can be combined with | (OR), & (AND) and ~ (NOT).
Refers to a column’s value inside the database, for updates and comparisons.
One query for a list plus one more for each row’s related object.
Fetches foreign-key objects in the same query using a SQL JOIN.

lessons.examTip: Know the difference: select_related uses a JOIN and works for ForeignKey and OneToOne; prefetch_related runs a second query and joins in Python, for reverse FKs and ManyToMany.

steps: With the seeded BookIt database, open python manage.py shell and paste snippets/orm_reports.py section by section.
Print todays.query and read the JOIN that select_related produced.
Run the N+1 measurement and note both numbers.
Write a query for revenue per staff member this month, highest first, using annotate and Sum with a filter.
Write a query for the cancellation rate per service (cancelled / total) using two Count annotations.
check: The N+1 test prints 101 without select_related and 1 with it.

lessons.title: Business rules in a service layer
lessons.summaryHtml: Where the booking rules live: services.py functions shared by the web dashboard and the API, transaction.atomic, select_for_update to stop double booking, and the overlap test.
lessons.contentHtml:
Why a service layer

BookIt has two front doors: the staff dashboard and the mobile API. If the “no double booking” rule lived in a view, the API would not have it. Business rules go in plain functions in services.py. Views and serializers only call them.

class BookingError(Exception):
    """A business rule was violated. The message is safe to show users."""

Creating a booking safely

@transaction.atomic
def create_booking(*, customer, service: Service, start_at: datetime, staff=None, notes: str = "") -> Booking:
    # Lock the service row: two people clicking "Book" for the same slot at the
    # same moment are now processed one after the other, never both accepted.
    service = Service.objects.select_for_update().get(pk=service.pk)

    if not service.is_active:
        raise BookingError("This service is not available right now.")
    if start_at <= timezone.now():
        raise BookingError("Please choose a time in the future.")

    end_at = start_at + timedelta(minutes=service.duration_minutes)
    clash = Booking.objects.filter(
        service=service,
        status__in=Booking.ACTIVE_STATUSES,
        start_at__lt=end_at,  # overlap test: A.start < B.end AND A.end > B.start
        end_at__gt=start_at,
    ).exists()
    if clash:
        raise BookingError("That slot was just taken. Please pick another time.")

    return Booking.objects.create(..., price=service.price, ...)

The race condition

Without a lock, two customers can both run the clash check at the same instant, both see “free”, and both get booked. select_for_update() locks the service row until the transaction ends, so the second request waits, then sees the first booking and is rejected.

select_for_update() only works inside a transaction, which is why the function is wrapped in @transaction.atomic. On SQLite it does nothing; it needs PostgreSQL, which is what production uses.

The overlap test

Two time ranges overlap when A starts before B ends AND A ends after B starts. That one condition covers every case: partly before, partly after, inside, around. Back-to-back bookings (10:00–11:00 and 11:00–12:00) do not clash because the comparisons are strict.

Changing status

@transaction.atomic
def change_status(*, booking: Booking, new_status: str, by) -> Booking:
    booking = Booking.objects.select_for_update().get(pk=booking.pk)
    if not booking.can_transition_to(new_status):
        raise BookingError(f"A {booking.get_status_display().lower()} booking cannot become '{new_status}'.")
    if not by.is_staff_member and booking.customer_id != by.pk:
        raise BookingError("You can only change your own bookings.")
    booking.status = new_status
    booking.save(update_fields=["status", "updated_at"])
    return booking

save(update_fields=[...]) writes only those columns, so it cannot overwrite a field another request just changed.

Free slots

available_slots() fetches the taken ranges for the day in one query, then walks the opening hours in 30-minute steps and keeps slots in the future that overlap nothing. All times are timezone-aware (USE_TZ = True, TIME_ZONE = "Asia/Kolkata").

Locks the selected rows until the transaction ends, so concurrent requests wait their turn.

options: The API and the dashboard both call the same function, so the rules are written and tested once
quiz.explanation: One function, two callers. A rule in a view would be missing from the API.

quiz.question: What does select_for_update() protect against in create_booking?
options: Two simultaneous requests both seeing the slot as free and both booking it
quiz.explanation: The lock makes the second request wait until the first commits, then its clash check sees the new booking.

quiz.explanation: 10:30 < 11:00 and 11:30 > 10:00, so it overlaps. Back-to-back slots do not.

quiz.question: Why save(update_fields=["status", "updated_at"])?

quiz.explanation: A plain save() writes every column from the in-memory object, which can undo someone else’s change.

lessons.title: The staff dashboard
lessons.summaryHtml: Server-rendered pages with class-based views: a KPI home page, a searchable, filterable, paginated booking list, POST-only status changes with messages, and ModelForms with custom validation.
lessons.contentHtml:
Why we don’t give clients the Django admin

Django adminCustom dashboard
Generic look, hard to brandBranded, modern UI
Exposes every modelShows only what that role needs
Model-level permissionsBusiness-level permissions
Workflows (approve, assign, refund) are awkwardBusiness actions are buttons that call service functions, with the same rules as the API

The brief: the car wash manager opens the dashboard every morning on a laptop at the counter. They need today’s numbers at a glance, to find a customer by phone in two seconds, and to move bookings through their workflow without mistakes.

Who may see it

class StaffRequiredMixin(LoginRequiredMixin, UserPassesTestMixin):
    """Logged-in AND role is admin/staff. Customers get 403, guests go to login."""

    def test_func(self):
        return self.request.user.is_staff_member

Every dashboard view lists this mixin first. Login alone is not enough: a customer who logs in must get 403, not the business numbers.

KPIs in get_context_data

class DashboardHomeView(StaffRequiredMixin, TemplateView):
    template_name = "dashboard/home.html"

    def get_context_data(self, **kwargs):
        ctx = super().get_context_data(**kwargs)
        ...
        ctx["kpis"] = {
            "today": bookings.filter(start_at__date=today).count(),
            "pending": bookings.filter(status=Booking.Status.PENDING).count(),
            "month_revenue": completed_this_month.aggregate(total=Sum("price"))["total"] or 0,
            "month_completed": completed_this_month.count(),
        }
        ctx["upcoming"] = (...).select_related("customer", "service", "staff").order_by("start_at")[:8]

Note or 0: Sum over no rows is None, not 0.

A list with search, filter and pagination

class BookingListView(StaffRequiredMixin, ListView):
    template_name = "dashboard/bookings/list.html"
    context_object_name = "bookings"
    paginate_by = 20

    def get_queryset(self):
        qs = Booking.objects.select_related("customer", "service", "staff")
        q = self.request.GET.get("q", "").strip()
        status = self.request.GET.get("status", "")
        if q:
            qs = qs.filter(Q(customer__first_name__icontains=q) | Q(customer__phone__icontains=q) | Q(service__name__icontains=q))
        if status in Booking.Status.values:
            qs = qs.filter(status=status)
        return qs

Only known statuses are applied (status in Booking.Status.values), so a tampered URL cannot cause an error. In the template, keep q and status in the pagination links so page 2 keeps the filter.

Changes are POST only

@require_POST
@login_required
def booking_change_status(request, pk):
    if not request.user.is_staff_member:
        raise PermissionDenied
    booking = get_object_or_404(Booking, pk=pk)
    try:
        change_status(booking=booking, new_status=request.POST.get("status", ""), by=request.user)
        messages.success(request, "Booking status updated.")
    except BookingError as exc:
        messages.error(request, str(exc))
    return redirect("dashboard:booking-detail", pk=pk)

A GET link that changes data can be triggered by a browser prefetch or an image tag on another site. POST plus {% csrf_token %} prevents that. After the POST, redirect (Post/Redirect/Get) so a refresh does not submit again.

ModelForm with a custom rule

class ServiceForm(StyledFormMixin, forms.ModelForm):
    class Meta:
        model = Service
        fields = ["name", "slug", "description", "duration_minutes", "price", "gst_rate", "is_active"]

    def clean_duration_minutes(self):
        minutes = self.cleaned_data["duration_minutes"]
        if minutes % 15:
            raise forms.ValidationError("Duration must be in 15-minute steps.")
        return minutes

Always list fields explicitly. fields = "__all__" silently exposes every new column you add later. StyledFormMixin adds CSS classes to every widget so templates stay clean.

Django 5 only logs out on POST. That is why base.html has a small logout form with a button rather than a link.

Templates and URLs

  • Every URL file has an app_name; templates use {% url 'dashboard:booking-list' %}. Never hard-code paths: if a prefix changes, reversed names keep working.
  • One base.html with blocks; every page {% extends %} it.
  • Django auto-escapes variables, so XSS is blocked by default. Never use |safe on user input.
  • {% querystring page=... %} (Django 5.1+) keeps the search and filter parameters when paging.
  • The Tailwind CDN is fine for training. In production, build the CSS with the Tailwind CLI and serve the file.

Middleware and signals: use carefully

Middleware suits cross-cutting concerns: timing, audit logs, tenant detection in white-label SaaS. Signals (post_save) hide logic and make code hard to follow; prefer explicit calls in the service layer. If you do send an email or notification, do it in transaction.on_commit(...) so you never notify about a booking that was rolled back.

Acceptance criteria

  • No django.contrib.admin in INSTALLED_APPS.
  • The bookings list runs at most 3 queries per page (check with django-debug-toolbar).
  • Status changes go through services.change_status only.
  • Works on a 13" laptop and at mobile width.

Stretch goals: a 14-day revenue bar chart (Chart.js); CSV export of the filtered bookings; assign staff from the detail page.

quiz.question: Why does StaffRequiredMixin check role as well as login?
options: A logged-in customer must not see business data
quiz.explanation: Authentication says who you are; authorisation says what you may do. The dashboard needs both.

quiz.question: Why is changing a booking’s status a POST and not a GET link?
options: GET requests can be triggered by prefetching or other sites; POST with CSRF protection cannot
quiz.explanation: State-changing actions must use POST so the CSRF token protects them.

quiz.question: Sum("price") over a month with no completed bookings returns…
quiz.explanation: SQL SUM over no rows is NULL, which Django returns as None. Hence the or 0.

quiz.explanation: on_commit runs only after the transaction succeeds, so nobody is told about a booking that was rolled back. The service layer keeps the logic visible.

It does not work with ModelForm

lessons.title: A REST API with DRF and JWT
lessons.summaryHtml: The API the mobile app uses: register and JWT login, serializers that read nested and write by id, viewsets with a custom action, per-user querysets that prevent IDOR, one error shape, throttling and Swagger docs.
lessons.contentHtml:
Endpoints

Method and pathWhat it does
POST /api/v1/auth/register/Create a customer account
POST /api/v1/auth/token/Log in: returns access and refresh tokens
POST /api/v1/auth/token/refresh/New access token from a refresh token
GET /api/v1/services/Public list, with search and ordering
GET /api/v1/services/<slug>/slots/?date=Free slots for a day
GET/POST /api/v1/bookings/My bookings / book a slot
POST /api/v1/bookings/<id>/cancel/Cancel my booking
GET /api/v1/docs/Swagger UI generated by drf-spectacular

REST rules we follow

  • Version from day one (/api/v1/). Mobile apps in the Play Store cannot be force-updated.
  • Plural nouns for resources; verbs only for actions (/cancel/).
  • Status codes: 400 validation, 401 not logged in, 403 not allowed, 404 not found or not yours, 429 throttled.
  • The default permission is IsAuthenticated, so every endpoint is private unless you open it on purpose.
  • CORS allows only your own frontends (e.g. the Next.js app), never * in production.

JWT in one paragraph

The app sends username and password once and receives a short-lived access token (30 minutes) and a longer refresh token (7 days). Every request carries Authorization: Bearer <access>. When it expires, the app swaps the refresh token for a new pair; with rotation and blacklisting, an old refresh token cannot be reused.

Serializers: nested on read, id on write

class BookingSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):
    service = ServiceSerializer(read_only=True)  # nested on read
    service_id = serializers.PrimaryKeyRelatedField(  # plain id on write
        queryset=Service.objects.filter(is_active=True), source="service", write_only=True
    )
    status_display = serializers.CharField(source="get_status_display", read_only=True)

    class Meta:
        model = Booking
        fields = ["id", "service", "service_id", "start_at", "end_at",
                  "status", "status_display", "price", "notes", "created_at"]
        read_only_fields = ["end_at", "status", "price", "created_at"]

    def create(self, validated_data):
        try:
            return create_booking(customer=self.context["request"].user, **validated_data)
        except BookingError as exc:
            raise serializers.ValidationError({"start_at": [str(exc)]}) from exc

price and status are read-only: a client must never send its own price. The customer comes from the token, not the request body. The serializer calls the same create_booking as the dashboard.

Only your own rows: preventing IDOR

def get_queryset(self):
    qs = Booking.objects.select_related("service")
    user = self.request.user
    # Customers only ever see their own rows -> no IDOR (guessing /bookings/42/)
    return qs if user.is_staff_member else qs.filter(customer=user)

Because retrieve, list and the cancel action all start from this queryset, another customer’s booking returns 404, not 403. The API does not even confirm it exists.

A custom action

@action(detail=True, methods=["post"])
def cancel(self, request, pk=None):
    booking = self.get_object()
    try:
        booking = change_status(booking=booking, new_status=Booking.Status.CANCELLED, by=request.user)
    except BookingError as exc:
        return Response({"success": False, "errors": {"detail": str(exc)}}, status=status.HTTP_400_BAD_REQUEST)
    return Response(self.get_serializer(booking).data)

One error shape for every endpoint

def api_exception_handler(exc, context):
    response = exception_handler(exc, context)
    if response is not None:
        response.data = {"success": False, "status_code": response.status_code, "errors": response.data}
    return response

The Flutter app can always read response["errors"], whatever went wrong. Settings also add default pagination (20 per page), filtering, and throttling (30/min anonymous, 120/min per user).

The booking viewset deliberately has no update or delete mixins. Customers cancel through the cancel action so the state machine always runs.

The brief: mobile API for the Flutter app

Our Flutter developer starts the customer app on Monday. They need a stable, documented API and a Postman or Bruno collection today. Deliver: every endpoint above working with JWT; Swagger listing all of them; a GET/PATCH /api/v1/me/ profile endpoint; an exported collection in docs/ with variables for the base URL and token.

Stretch goals: GET /bookings/{id}/invoice/ using Day 2’s invoice.py for the GST totals; a staff-only /api/v1/staff/bookings/; cursor pagination for an infinite-scroll list.

terms.definition: Converts model instances to JSON and validates incoming JSON.
One class providing list, retrieve, create and other actions, wired to URLs by a router.
A signed token carrying the user id. Access tokens are short-lived; refresh tokens get new ones.
Insecure Direct Object Reference: reading someone else’s data by changing an id in the URL.
Adds a custom endpoint such as /bookings/<id>/cancel/ to a ViewSet.
Limiting how many requests a client can make per minute.
A machine-readable description of the API and an interactive page to try it.

lessons.examTip: For any API that returns user data, the first security question is “can user A read user B’s rows by changing the id?”. Filtering get_queryset by request.user is the standard answer.

quiz.explanation: get_queryset only contains the customer’s own bookings, so 42 is simply not found. This also hides whether it exists.

quiz.question: Why are price and status read_only in BookingSerializer?
options: They are computed by the database
Clients must not set their own price or skip the status rules
quiz.explanation: The server decides the price (snapshot of the service) and status changes go through the state machine.

quiz.question: What is the refresh token for?
options: Getting a new access token without asking for the password again
quiz.explanation: Access tokens are short-lived for safety. The refresh token renews them; with rotation each refresh gives a new refresh token.

quiz.question: Why not set CORS to allow * in production?
options: Any website’s scripts could then call your API from your users’ browsers
quiz.explanation: CORS is the browser rule for which sites may call your API from JavaScript. List only your own frontends.

quiz.question: Why does the API start at /api/v1/?
options: Installed mobile apps cannot be force-updated, so old versions must keep working when the API changes
quiz.explanation: With a version in the path you can ship /api/v2/ without breaking phones still running the old app.

quiz.question: Why does the serializer’s create() call create_booking() instead of Booking.objects.create()?
options: So the API gets the same locking, overlap and price rules as the dashboard
quiz.explanation: The service layer is the single home of the booking rules.

lessons.title: API tests and seed data
lessons.summaryHtml: pytest-django tests that prove the business rules through the real API, and a seed_demo management command that fills the database with realistic demo data in one fast query.
lessons.contentHtml:
Testing through the API

These tests use the real URLs, real serializers and a real test database. They prove what the mobile app will see.

def test_booking_snapshots_price_and_blocks_double_booking(api, customer, other_customer, service):
    payload = {"service_id": service.id, "start_at": tomorrow_at(10).isoformat()}

    api.force_authenticate(customer)
    r = api.post("/api/v1/bookings/", payload, format="json")
    assert r.status_code == 201, r.data
    assert r.data["price"] == "499.00"
    assert r.data["status"] == "pending"

    api.force_authenticate(other_customer)
    r = api.post("/api/v1/bookings/", payload, format="json")
    assert r.status_code == 400
    assert r.data["success"] is False
  • The db fixture (pulled in by customer and service) gives each test a clean database.
  • force_authenticate skips the token dance when the test is not about login.
  • assert r.status_code == 201, r.data prints the error body when it fails.
  • Test what the business cares about: the price snapshot, double booking blocked, privacy (404), state rules.
pip install -r requirements/dev.txt
pytest -q      # pytest.ini sets DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=config.settings.dev
# expected: 5 passed

Try it like the Flutter developer will

curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/v1/auth/token/ \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"username": "anu", "password": "demo12345"}'
# copy "access" from the answer, then:
curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/v1/bookings/ -H "Authorization: Bearer <access>"

Seed data with a management command

Every project needs realistic demo data for client demos and for testing the dashboard. Write a command; don’t click data in by hand.

class Command(BaseCommand):
    help = "Create demo services, staff, customers and bookings"

    def add_arguments(self, parser):
        parser.add_argument("--bookings", type=int, default=200)

    @transaction.atomic
    def handle(self, *args, **options):
        services = [Service.objects.get_or_create(slug=slugify(name), defaults={...})[0] for ...]
        ...
        # bulk_create = one INSERT instead of hundreds (seed data only; skips overlap rules)
        Booking.objects.bulk_create(bookings, batch_size=500)

get_or_create makes the command safe to run twice. bulk_create is fast because it skips save() and your service-layer rules, so use it only for demo or migration data.

terms.definition: pytest plugin that sets up Django and provides fixtures such as db and client.
DRF’s test client for calling API endpoints with JSON and authentication.
Makes APIClient act as a given user without a real token.
A custom python manage.py <name> command in an app’s management/commands folder.
Inserts many rows in few queries, skipping save() and signals.
Safe to run more than once with the same result.

lessons.examTip: A good API test reads like a user story: who calls, what they send, what they must get back. Name it after the rule it proves.

options: So running the command twice does not create duplicates
quiz.explanation: Idempotent seed commands can be run again safely.

quiz.question: What does bulk_create skip?

quiz.explanation: bulk_create inserts directly, so custom save logic and signals do not run. Fine for seed data, not for real bookings.

options: It skips getting a token when the test is about something else
It is required for every request

quiz.explanation: Test the business and security rules, not trivial getters.

lessons.title: Production, security and deploying on Railway
lessons.summaryHtml: Code on a laptop has no value to a client. Harden BookIt with production settings and the security checklist, deploy it on Railway with PostgreSQL, and learn the Ralfiz Git workflow.
lessons.contentHtml:
Production settings

DEBUG = False
CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS = env.list("CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS", default=[])

# Railway terminates TLS at its proxy and forwards X-Forwarded-Proto
SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER = ("HTTP_X_FORWARDED_PROTO", "https")
SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT = env.bool("SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT", default=True)
SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE = True
CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE = True
SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS = env.int("SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS", default=3600)  # raise to 31536000 once stable
X_FRAME_OPTIONS = "DENY"

Railway handles HTTPS at its proxy and talks plain HTTP to your app. SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER tells Django to trust the proxy’s header; without it SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT redirects forever. Start HSTS small and raise it once HTTPS works everywhere, because browsers remember it.

Security checklist (every project, every time)

  • DEBUG=False, with a long random SECRET_KEY from env vars (never in Git).
  • ALLOWED_HOSTS and CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS set to the real domains.
  • HTTPS redirect, secure cookies, HSTS.
  • Every queryset scoped to the user (IDOR); every endpoint has explicit permissions.
  • Login and register throttled.
  • Uploads validated for extension and size, and never served from the code directory.
  • No |safe on user content; no raw SQL built with string formatting.
  • CORS restricted to known frontends.
  • Dependencies pinned; pip-audit run before release.

Deploy on Railway

  1. Add requirements.txt at the root containing -r requirements/prod.txt, and pin Python with a .python-version file (e.g. 3.12).
  2. Push to GitHub. In Railway: New Project → Deploy from GitHub repo.
  3. Add a PostgreSQL database to the project.
  4. In the web service’s Variables add DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=config.settings.prod, SECRET_KEY, DATABASE_URL (a reference to the Postgres service), ALLOWED_HOSTS and CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS.
  5. In Settings → Deploy set the pre-deploy command python manage.py migrate and the start command python manage.py collectstatic --noinput && gunicorn config.wsgi.
  6. Generate a public domain under Settings → Networking, then create the first admin with railway run python manage.py createsuperuser and set their role to admin.
Common deploy errors. 400 Bad Request → ALLOWED_HOSTS. CSRF failed on login → CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS needs https://. Static files 404 → WhiteNoise middleware order or collectstatic. Redirect loop → SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER. Always read the deploy logs first.

For client projects the domain is bought on Namecheap and pointed to Railway with a CNAME record from the service’s custom-domain settings. Add the new domain to ALLOWED_HOSTS and CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS. Railway’s disk is wiped on every deploy, so uploaded media needs a volume or object storage.

Performance and observability basics

  • Measure before optimising: django-debug-toolbar in dev, the slow-request middleware in prod.
  • Queries: select_related/prefetch_related, indexes on filtered columns, .only() for heavy tables, and always paginate.
  • Caching: cache expensive, rarely-changing data (the service list, dashboard KPIs for 60 seconds) with Redis via Django’s cache framework.
  • Background work: emails, SMS, WhatsApp messages and PDF invoices should not run inside the request. Use a task queue (Celery or RQ with Redis) once a project needs it.
  • Errors: connect an error tracker (e.g. Sentry) so you hear about crashes before the client does.

The Ralfiz Git workflow

Pull request checklist: small PR (under about 400 lines, one purpose); tests added and green; migrations included and reviewed; no secrets, prints or commented-out code; screenshots for UI changes.
